## order-state.ts (core)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typestate
 * @options 5e58ab21f878d2ed
 */

/**
 * The states, and the order they occur in.
 *
 * Written out here as well as in each interface, because it is what the shared
 * operations are keyed by.
 */
export type OrderState = "draft" | "submitted" | "paid";

/**
 * Still being assembled. Items can be added; nothing downstream can see it yet.
 *
 * The state field is a literal, which is what separates these types from one
 * another and lets a value of unknown state be narrowed. It is also the
 * pattern's weak point in this representation: an interface can be satisfied by
 * any object literal, so nothing stops a caller writing a paid order into
 * existence and skipping the workflow entirely. The parameterised
 * representation closes that with a private constructor; here the operations
 * are guarded and the states are not.
 */
export interface OrderDraft {
  readonly state: "draft";
  readonly items: readonly string[];
}

/**
 * Fixed and awaiting payment. The contents are settled, so adding to it is no
 * longer meaningful.
 */
export interface OrderSubmitted {
  readonly state: "submitted";
  readonly items: readonly string[];
}

/**
 * Settled. The only remaining operation is undoing it.
 */
export interface OrderPaid {
  readonly state: "paid";
  readonly items: readonly string[];
}

/**
 * Order in any state, for the operations that do not care which.
 *
 * Narrowing by the state field works on this in the ordinary way, since it is
 * an ordinary discriminated union.
 */
export type AnyOrder = OrderDraft | OrderSubmitted | OrderPaid;

/**
 * A value whose transition has already been taken.
 *
 * Not a defensive check against a caller doing something absurd. It is the
 * pattern's one genuine gap: a transition supersedes its input, and there is no
 * way to say so in TypeScript, so this is where that constraint is enforced
 * instead.
 */
export class StaleOrderError extends Error {
  readonly state: OrderState;

  constructor(state: OrderState) {
    super(`this order has already left the "${state}" state`);
    this.name = "StaleOrderError";
    this.state = state;
  }
}

/**
 * Values that have already been transitioned.
 *
 * A `WeakSet` rather than a flag on the value, for two reasons that both
 * matter. The types stay `readonly`, so nothing about the guard leaks into the
 * shape a caller sees or has to serialise. And entries do not keep their keys
 * alive, so a long-running process that transitions many values does not
 * accumulate them here.
 */
const consumed = new WeakSet<object>();

/**
 * Records that this value's transition has been taken, refusing a second one.
 *
 * Called by the transitions only. An operation that stays in its state derives
 * a new value and leaves the original perfectly usable, which is ordinary value
 * semantics and not something to guard against — what is guarded is a *state
 * change* being taken twice.
 */
function take(subject: AnyOrder): void {
  if (consumed.has(subject)) {
    throw new StaleOrderError(subject.state);
  }

  consumed.add(subject);
}

/**
 * The only way in.
 *
 * A function rather than a literal at each call site, so that the initial state
 * is written once. It is not a barrier, though — see the note on the first
 * interface: an object literal can produce any of these states directly.
 */
export function draft(): OrderDraft {
  return { state: "draft", items: [] };
}

/**
 * How many items, whatever the state.
 *
 * Takes `AnyOrder`, which is what makes it callable on every state.
 */
export function count(order: AnyOrder): number {
  return order.items.length;
}

/**
 * Adds an item, staying in draft.
 *
 * The parameter type is the constraint. It derives a new value rather than
 * transitioning, so the argument is not consumed.
 */
export function add(order: OrderDraft, item: string): OrderDraft {
  return { state: "draft", items: [...order.items, item] };
}

/**
 * draft → submitted.
 *
 * A transition, so the result supersedes the argument, and `take` enforces that
 * because the type system cannot.
 */
export function submit(order: OrderDraft): OrderSubmitted {
  take(order);

  return { state: "submitted", items: order.items };
}

/**
 * submitted → paid.
 */
export function pay(order: OrderSubmitted): OrderPaid {
  take(order);

  return { state: "paid", items: order.items };
}

/**
 * Only once paid.
 */
export function refund(order: OrderPaid): string {
  return `refunded ${String(order.items.length)} items`;
}
```

## order-state-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typestate
 * @options 5e58ab21f878d2ed
 */

/**
 * Working through the states, and the operations each one refuses.
 *
 * The refusals at the end are assertions, not illustrations: `@ts-expect-error`
 * is satisfied by an error and violated by silence, so each states that the
 * line below it must not compile. This file is emitted whether or not tests
 * were asked for, because "the wrong operation is uncallable" is the whole
 * claim and an unasserted claim is a hope.
 *
 * A directive governs the line it begins on, so where the refused expression is
 * an initialiser it sits between the `=` and the expression rather than above
 * the statement. Above the statement it holds only while the statement fits one
 * line: a long enough type name pushes the expression down, the error is
 * reported there, and the assertion inverts into two errors — the escaped
 * mistake, and a directive suppressing nothing.
 */

import { add, count, draft, pay, refund, submit } from "./order-state.js";
import type {
  AnyOrder,
  OrderDraft,
  OrderPaid,
  OrderSubmitted,
} from "./order-state.js";

/**
 * The whole workflow, in the order it has to happen.
 *
 * Each step's return type is the only thing the next accepts, so the order is
 * forced. The cost of this representation is visible here — the steps nest or
 * need naming, where methods would chain — and naming them is also what makes a
 * stale value easy to reach for, since the earlier bindings stay in scope and
 * stay valid.
 */
export function settle(): string {
  const assembled = add(add(draft(), "widget"), "gasket");
  const awaitingPayment = submit(assembled);
  const settled = pay(awaitingPayment);

  return refund(settled);
}

/**
 * An operation that does not care about the state.
 */
export function describe(subject: AnyOrder): string {
  return `${subject.state}: ${String(count(subject))} items`;
}

/**
 * Recovering a specific state from a value that could be in any of them.
 *
 * An ordinary discriminated union, narrowed in the ordinary way.
 */
export function addIfStillOpen(subject: AnyOrder, item: string): AnyOrder {
  if (subject.state === "draft") {
    return add(subject, item);
  }

  return subject;
}

/**
 * Narrowing to the far end works the same way, which is what makes `paid`-only
 * operations reachable from a value of unknown state.
 */
export function refundIfSettled(subject: AnyOrder): string | undefined {
  return subject.state === "paid" ? refund(subject) : undefined;
}

/**
 * The limit, shown rather than asserted.
 *
 * Nothing here is a compile error, and that is the point: a transition
 * supersedes its input, TypeScript has no way to say so, and both calls below
 * are as valid to the compiler as any other. The second one throws
 * `StaleOrderError` at run time, which is the only place the constraint can
 * live.
 */
export function theSameValueTwice(): void {
  const first = draft();

  void submit(first);
  void submit(first);
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * Each directive sits alone on its line with the reason above it, because a
 * directive governs only the line it begins on and a long comment gets
 * re-wrapped by the formatter.
 */

export function refusesAddingAfterSubmission(): void {
  const fixed = submit(draft());

  // The contents are settled once submitted, so `add` is not part of that
  // state.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  void add(fixed, "late");
}

export function refusesSkippingAState(): void {
  // pay arrives from submitted, never from draft. The workflow's order is the
  // type's.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  void pay(draft());
}

export function refusesRefundingBeforePayment(): void {
  const fixed = submit(draft());

  // @ts-expect-error there is nothing to refund yet
  void refund(fixed);
}

export function refusesCrossStateAssignment(): void {
  const open = draft();

  // The states are separate types, not one type with a changing field. This is
  // the assignment the anchoring field exists to reject — without it the
  // instantiations are identical and it succeeds.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  const fixed: OrderSubmitted = open;

  void fixed;
}
```

## order-state.test-d.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typestate
 * @options 5e58ab21f878d2ed
 */

/**
 * What the compiler is asked to prove.
 *
 * Nothing here runs. The suffix keeps the file out of every runner while
 * leaving it in front of the compiler, which is the only thing that can check a
 * claim about a type — a workflow whose states had quietly become
 * interchangeable would behave identically at run time to one that had not.
 *
 * No claim below concerns nullability, since with `strictNullChecks` off
 * `undefined` is assignable to everything and such a claim would mean opposite
 * things to two different callers.
 */

import { draft, pay, submit } from "./order-state.js";
import type {
  AnyOrder,
  OrderDraft,
  OrderPaid,
  OrderSubmitted,
} from "./order-state.js";

/**
 * Forces its argument to be `true`, and fails to compile when it is not.
 *
 * Each assertion below is written as a named alias rather than a bare one, so
 * that it reads as a stated claim about the code and cannot be mistaken for a
 * leftover.
 */
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

/**
 * Whether two types are identical, rather than merely assignable in both
 * directions.
 *
 * The two-function form looks like a trick because it is one: it compares the
 * types in a position the compiler checks by identity instead of by
 * assignability. The obvious alternative — asking whether each extends the
 * other — answers a different question, and answers it wrongly in two common
 * cases. It reports `true` for `any` against anything at all, and it
 * distributes over unions, so a union compared against one of its own members
 * can come back true.
 */
export type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is assignable to `Y`.
 *
 * Both sides are wrapped in a tuple to stop the union distribution a bare
 * conditional performs. Undistributed is the question that was meant: whether
 * the whole of `X` is acceptable as a `Y`, rather than whether each member of
 * it is on its own.
 */
export type Extends<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? true : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is rejected where a `Y` is wanted.
 *
 * The type-level counterpart to `@ts-expect-error`, and preferable wherever the
 * claim is about a relationship rather than about a particular line: a
 * directive suppresses whichever error occurs, so it can be satisfied by an
 * unrelated mistake on the same line, where this cannot.
 */
export type NotAssignable<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? false : true;

/**
 * The states do not interchange.
 *
 * The claim the whole pattern rests on, and the one that fails silently: a
 * state parameter that no member mentions leaves these types structurally
 * identical, and then every constraint on every operation stops applying with
 * nothing to report it.
 */
export type OrderDraftIsNotOrderSubmitted = Expect<
  NotAssignable<OrderDraft, OrderSubmitted>
>;
export type OrderSubmittedIsNotOrderDraft = Expect<
  NotAssignable<OrderSubmitted, OrderDraft>
>;

/**
 * Each state belongs to the any-state type, which is what makes the shared
 * operations reachable.
 */
export type EveryStateBelongsToAnyOrder = Expect<
  Extends<OrderDraft | OrderSubmitted | OrderPaid, AnyOrder>
>;

/**
 * A transition's result is the next state exactly, not merely something
 * assignable to it.
 *
 * `Equal` rather than `Extends`, so that a transition widened to return the
 * any-state type — which would leave the caller unable to do anything specific
 * and is an easy accident — is caught.
 */
export type SubmitArrives = Expect<
  Equal<ReturnType<typeof submit>, OrderSubmitted>
>;
export type PayArrives = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof pay>, OrderPaid>>;
```

## order-state.test.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typestate
 * @options 5e58ab21f878d2ed
 */

/**
 * What is left for a suite that runs.
 *
 * Not which operations each state forbids — that is settled before this file
 * executes, and `order-state.test-d.ts` is where it is asserted. What remains
 * is the behaviour the types say nothing about: that items survive the
 * transitions, and that reusing a superseded value is refused.
 */

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import {
  StaleOrderError,
  add,
  count,
  draft,
  pay,
  refund,
  submit,
} from "./order-state.js";

describe("the workflow", () => {
  it("carries the items through every transition", () => {
    // The transitions rebuild the value, so this is the assertion that they
    // rebuild it faithfully — an easy thing to get wrong in a way no type would
    // notice, since every state has the same field.
    const assembled = add(add(draft(), "widget"), "gasket");
    const fixed = submit(assembled);
    const settled = pay(fixed);

    expect(count(assembled)).toBe(2);
    expect(count(fixed)).toBe(2);
    expect(count(settled)).toBe(2);
    expect(settled.items).toEqual(["widget", "gasket"]);
  });

  it("records the state it has reached", () => {
    const assembled = add(add(draft(), "widget"), "gasket");

    expect(assembled.state).toBe("draft");
    expect(submit(assembled).state).toBe("submitted");
  });

  it("reaches the end", () => {
    const settled = pay(submit(add(add(draft(), "widget"), "gasket")));

    expect(refund(settled)).toBe("refunded 2 items");
  });
});

describe("a superseded value", () => {
  // The one thing here that types cannot express, so the only part of the
  // pattern a run-time suite is solely responsible for.
  it("is refused on a second transition", () => {
    const open = draft();
    void submit(open);

    expect(() => submit(open)).toThrow(/already left/);
  });

  it("names the state it had already left", () => {
    const open = draft();
    void submit(open);

    let caught: unknown;
    try {
      void submit(open);
    } catch (error) {
      caught = error;
    }

    expect(caught instanceof StaleOrderError).toBe(true);
    expect((caught as StaleOrderError).state).toBe("draft");
  });

  it("does not refuse an operation that stays in its state", () => {
    // `add` derives a new value and does not transition, so neither the input
    // nor the result is spent. Guarding it would break ordinary immutable
    // updates.
    const open = draft();
    const withOne = add(open, "widget");

    expect(count(add(withOne, "gasket"))).toBe(2);

    // Asserted by reaching the next state rather than by the absence of a
    // throw: it establishes the same thing and says what happened instead of
    // what did not.
    expect(submit(withOne).state).toBe("submitted");
  });
});
```
